Father Mohan cannot cook. He has told me so himself, three times, while standing in my cellar up to his shins in Nile water and asking about my mother's lentil bread. I said the recipe went into the ground with her, which was not a lie, exactly, since she never measured anything and I only ever watched. He nodded and lifted another sack of flour onto the shelf above the waterline. For a man who preaches at me every feast day, he carries flour poorly; half of it was paste by noon. When he had gone, I found the sacks stacked by weight, the ruined ones set apart, and a pencil note on the lid of the bread tin asking only what she had used in place of salt. I kept the note. On Sunday, I set a loaf on the vestry step before the bells, and went home by the long road so as not to pass his door.

Flour dust on the counter showed every mark of Astrid's borrowed fountain pen, which she had been tapping since six. I had lent it to her at the notary's office in March, for one signature, and I reminded her of this whenever we met, usually while she was mispronouncing 'gracias' to someone who spoke perfect English. Two bakers share my scale. Every morning before I open, Wira and Arisa come through the back door of the shop with their sacks, and each accuses the other of resting a thumb on the brass pan. I have watched this for six years from behind a bolt of silk. They weigh, they quarrel about the weight, they leave by separate doors. On the wall above the scale someone keeps a chalk tally in two columns, and I have never asked whose hand it is. Last winter Arisa went to her sister's in Hai Phong for a month. Wira came at the usual hour, weighed his flour, and then, without a word to me, weighed out a second sack and set it by the door Arisa always used. He frowned at the pan for a long while, lifted his thumb from the edge, and weighed it again. Each morning the second column on the wall grew by one mark.

I did not mention the plum tree by the gate, which had died in March and which I had replaced, at my own cost, with one from a nursery in Songjiang. In my coat that day was a folded receipt that I kept meaning to throw away. A year later we met at the same table. Ayesha slid a photograph across to me: her uncle, young, beside the gate, the plum tree behind him already thick and crooked. She asked whether I thought a tree could straighten itself with age. I said some did. She nodded, put the photograph back in her bag, and ordered us both another pot.

By the autumn of 1931 the ranger Eunseo had given up the mountain and taken the job of marking the school field in lime. Eleven years earlier she had found a hiker named Bokhee in the fog below the crater, half a day off the trail, and had walked him down without once letting go of his collar, saying in front of the whole village that a fool deserved the fog. He had left the island the next week. She still kept, in her coat, the collar button that had come off in her hand. At dusk one evening a man came onto the field with a dozen boys and a ball. He set them in a row along her fresh white line and told them that anyone who crossed it before the whistle would run the field twice. Eunseo started toward him, the words she had saved ready in her mouth. Bokhee raised his hand to her, then blew his own whistle, and the boys ran.

The pool was cut into the rocks below the fort, and the tide refreshed it twice a day, and the water was green and very still. I had prepared a little speech about courage. I did not give it. I sat on the warm rock with my boots still laced and my hand on his towel until his head came up the third time.

Paper rattled on the drying lines, and the yard smelled of flour paste. Dario, who had taught half the neighborhood to read before he took up kites, handed Camila a spool of string and told her to measure out thirty meters for the red one. She measured it, cut it, and tied it to the frame the way he had shown her when she was nine. He tested the knot with one tug and nodded. Years ago he had promised the boy next door a kite that would clear the church tower, and the boy had moved away before it was built. The red kite was for him; Dario had kept the address in a tin. When Camila came back that evening, the boxed kite stood by the gate, and Dario was winding the leftover string onto the empty spool by hand, slowly, end to end, instead of throwing it out as he did with every other scrap. He set the spool in her palm and closed her fingers over it.

problem.passage:
What does a carpenter owe a bench that has outlived its builder? Wilhelmina asked that once, years ago, and Aroha had only handed her a block plane. That morning on the Maui promenade the plane did its ordinary work: Aroha shaved the warped slats of the old benches facing the harbor, and Wilhelmina swept the curls into a bucket. At the sixth bench Aroha stopped. Carved under the armrest were initials and a date, worn soft by salt. She ran the plane along the seat but lifted it each time it neared the letters, leaving a narrow strip untouched, a little higher than the rest. Wilhelmina's old shop teacher had told her she would never be careful enough for fine work, and she had repeated this to Aroha on her first day. At noon Aroha wiped the blade, set the plane in Wilhelmina's hands, and walked to the seventh bench without looking back.

problem.passage:
I had clerked for Judge Eamon for one summer when he invited me to his terrace above the Saône and announced, as if testing the sound of my name, that Takoda and he would finish the Ferrand file that week. __He kept the file's last page face down beneath a stone ashtray, as he had on the bench, where he never read a verdict until he had heard every word.__ We worked through the mornings. He corrected my French, poured the coffee himself, and pointed out which slope of vines belonged to which cousin. By Friday the other pages were annotated in his small slanted hand, and nothing remained to be heard. When I reached for the ashtray, he covered it with his palm, asked about my plans for autumn, and suggested I carry the file back to the court with the last page unread, just as it was.
